How it’s calculated
A straight-line trend uses completed days with full records, excluding today. It describes change within this period, not versus the previous period.
Ratings are compared within each session after removing its average score. Each session has equal total weight. No fixed mood baseline is assumed.
Compares app use between consecutive ratings in the same session, accounting for starting mood, total active time and elapsed time. Other apps form a combined comparison group.

Patterns show associations, not causes or diagnoses.
Learn how we analyze your records

We start with the records you choose: phone use and your 1–10 mood ratings. We summarize what happened, compare days or sessions with enough data, and show a trend only when the records support one. Missing data is left missing, rather than treated as zero. A pattern is a clue to notice, not proof that phone use caused a mood change.
How PhoneMood calculates your data
Back to trends
Close explanation
PhoneMood combines your phone-use records and mood ratings to look for patterns that repeat for you.
1. How long you used your phone
We summarize active phone time by day: your daily average, your usual range, and days that were clearly higher or lower. These numbers describe recorded use only; they do not infer your mood.
2. How use and mood may relate

For each rating, we look at use during an earlier window, such as the previous hour, and compare lower-use with higher-use records. We also account for your previous mood, time of day and missing coverage. A result might say that when use rose from about 18 to 47 minutes, later ratings were 0.5 points lower on average. That estimate comes from your records.
3. Which factors are worth noticing

We look at app minutes, continuous-use length, app switches, number of apps and late-night use. For an app, we compare its time with other apps while holding overall phone use roughly similar: did ratings differ when more time went to this app?
4. Why results use points of mood

Twenty app minutes, 30 switches and late-night use have different units. We translate them into one understandable number: the average mood-score difference between your usual lower and higher levels. We show up to three supported patterns and do not fill the list with unstable findings.
5. What pattern stability means

We consider how many days and valid ratings you have, whether the direction repeats, how uncertain the estimate is and whether coverage is complete. Early sign means limited data; fairly stable means repetition; stable means more data and consistency. We wait for at least 7 days and the minimum number of valid ratings before this analysis.
6. Why results change over time

PhoneMood uses your recent records. As new data arrives, your routines and patterns may change, so the estimates update. An update does not mean the earlier calculation was wrong; it means you have more information. The goal is to make hard-to-see patterns easier to understand.
